k97: Two questions decide an Albanian purchase, and neither is "which city is best". They are: what is the money for, and how much of it is there. This is our 2026 mapping of goal to zone across the country, followed by four worked allocations from 100,000 euros to a million. It is a framework for thinking, not investment advice, and the numbers carry the confidence levels we attach to them.
k98: Short-let in Durrës Plazh runs at roughly 7-11% gross, which is the strongest reliable return we track, and Vlorë produces the highest absolute monthly income at around 1,163 euros. Those are gross figures. After roughly 3-4% transaction costs, 15% tax on rental income, management and furnishing, the number you keep is considerably lower — still competitive by European standards, but not the headline.
k99: What is a realistic rental yield in Albania?
k100: Entry starts below 50,000 euros in Tale, Mali i Robit and Kombinat, though at that level legal checks matter more than location. Around 100,000 euros buys a one-bedroom short-let unit in Durrës Plazh or Qerret with a reserve for furnishing. Above 250,000 you can diversify between city long-let and coastal short-let rather than depending on one asset.
k101: How much do I need to invest in Albanian property?
k102: It depends on the type of letting. For year-round long-let, Tirana's Myslym Shyri and Don Bosko, because students, offices and steady employment do not have a season. For short-let, Durrës Plazh on gross yield and Vlorë on absolute income. Sarandë and Ksamil are better known and, at current prices, weaker on the arithmetic.
k103: Which Albanian city is best for rental income?
k104: Vlorë, on our assessment, because it functions as a city year-round and has hospitals. Sarandë has a milder winter but weaker medical infrastructure, which matters more with time. The common mistake is deciding after a summer visit, when both look equally good and neither is being tested.

k187: Where you buy in Albania gets discussed constantly. What you buy gets discussed far less, and it changes the risk profile more. Here is how we rate each property type in the Albanian market as of 2026 - off-plan against completed, new against old stock, penthouses, villas, townhouses and land - and what has to be true for each one to make sense.
k188: It carries a specific, structural risk: Albania has no escrow requirement, so your deposit goes to the developer rather than to a neutral third party, and if the project stalls you rank as an unsecured creditor. The 20-30% discount to a finished unit is the market pricing that risk rather than a bargain. It can work with a developer whose completion record you have verified yourself, and it is a poor choice for a first purchase.
k189: Is buying off-plan in Albania safe?
k190: It is the certificate of use — the document confirming a building was lawfully completed and may be occupied. A unit that holds one carries no construction risk, can be rented immediately and has a clean path to title. It is the single most useful thing to ask for by name, and "it is coming" is not an acceptable answer.
k191: What is leje përdorimi and why does it matter?
k192: Usually not in seismic zones. The discount on pre-2000 stock reflects genuine differences in construction standards, and the 2019 earthquake made that permanent rather than temporary. In central Tirana some older buildings are worth owning for the location and the plot; on the coast, in the areas that shook, we would not treat the discount as an opportunity.
k193: Are old apartments in Albania a bargain?
k194: It offers the largest upside available in this market and the largest chance of total loss. Title history, agricultural classification and unresolved restitution claims can each make a plot unbuildable or unsellable, and none are visible without legal research. It is viable only with a lawyer engaged before any money moves.
